Before budgeting your WhatsApp service replies, check which pricing page you are reading.

Two official Meta pages currently tell different stories.

The developer pricing documentation, updated September 30, describes an October 1, 2026 change: each business phone number gets a monthly allowance of 1,000 service messages, with service-message charges starting after that allowance is used. It also describes separate free-entry-point exceptions.

The general WhatsApp Business pricing page still says service replies within the 24-hour customer service window are free.

Those are not interchangeable statements. The service window determines when non-template replies can be sent; it should not be treated as proof that every reply is free under every pricing rule.

This is about the WhatsApp Business Platform/API—not a claim about every message sent from the WhatsApp Business app.

Before changing your budget, ask whoever manages your integration to confirm:

• Which current pricing rules apply to your Messaging account and business phone number.
• Which message categories were actually delivered, rather than merely sent.
• Which deliveries qualified for a free allowance or entry-point exception.
• How the billable deliveries reconcile with the invoice.

I would not turn conflicting documentation into a confident cost forecast. Check the applicable account terms and billing records first.

Does your WhatsApp report distinguish messages sent inside the service window from messages actually marked billable?

When building an AI Agent to handle order inquiries, there's one question I need to answer before letting it respond to customers

How does it know which order the customer is actually asking about

Let's say a customer sends a WhatsApp message asking where their order is

They have two open orders and haven't provided an order number

The Agent might understand the question perfectly and still pick the wrong order

It could end up sharing real tracking information from the system, but for a shipment that doesn't belong to that customer

And to me, that's more concerning than the Agent simply not knowing the answer

The customer has no way of knowing the Agent made a guess. They'll assume the information came directly from the system

That's why, if the Agent can't identify the right order, it should ask for the order number or another detail that helps narrow it down

Once it finds the order, it also needs to verify that it actually belongs to the customer before sharing any details

And if there's still uncertainty, it's better to hand the conversation over to a human than keep guessing

This is something I think about when designing AI Agents

Understanding the question isn't enough. There also need to be clear rules for when the Agent can make a decision, when it should ask for more information, and when it needs to stop and involve a human

Because in the end, a fast response isn't what matters most

Getting the right information to the right customer does

🚨 Your WhatsApp account could become a tool for cybercriminals. And the consequences can go far beyond losing access to your messages.
Recently, I've heard about several cases of people losing access to their WhatsApp accounts after receiving suspicious phone calls.
What makes these cases particularly concerning is that some victims report never sharing a verification code or clicking a suspicious link.
While answering an ordinary phone call does not normally compromise WhatsApp, these incidents deserve attention and investigation.
What can happen once a criminal takes control of your WhatsApp?
🔴 They can impersonate you and contact your friends, family, or colleagues.
🔴 They may add people to groups or use your identity to spread scams.
🔴 They may obtain access to sensitive information shared in new conversations or through other compromised devices and accounts.
🔴 If they obtain private photos, financial information, or confidential documents, they may use them for fraud, blackmail, or extortion.
🔴 They may threaten to publish sensitive material unless you pay them.
How can you protect yourself? 🔐
✅ Enable WhatsApp's two-step verification and create a strong, unique PIN.
✅ Add and verify a recovery email address.
✅ Set up a WhatsApp passkey if available on your device.
✅ Regularly check Settings → Linked Devices and remove unfamiliar sessions.
✅ Enable biometric protection and WhatsApp's app lock.
✅ Protect your voicemail with a strong PIN or disable it if unnecessary.
✅ Never share verification codes or approve unexpected device-linking requests.
✅ Keep your phone and WhatsApp updated.
Remember: Your WhatsApp is more than a messaging application. It's connected to your personal relationships, professional network, and digital identity.
Please take a few minutes today to review your security settings.
And if someone you know suddenly sends unusual requests for money or sensitive information, verify their identity through another trusted channel.
Cybersecurity starts with awareness. Protect yourself, and help others stay safe.

Official WhatsApp API, or a linked number? Pick before you build.

There are two ways to connect a business system to WhatsApp, and most of the confusion we see comes from people choosing one without knowing the other exists.

Meta's official platform: you register the number with Meta, get approved, and use Meta's API. Or you link the number you already use as a device, the way WhatsApp Web works. Threadwire is the second.

Neither is better. They're built for different jobs, and the wrong one is expensive either way. Choose official when you needed linked, and you'll wait on approvals and work inside templates you never needed. Choose linked when you needed official, and you're putting a number at risk for a use it was never safe for.

Nine images: what each gives you, what each costs you, and the rule of thumb we actually use.

The short version: if your customers write to you first — bookings, orders, support, reminders to people already in a chat — a linked number fits. If you need to reach more than 50 new people a day from one number, run campaigns, or want the verified badge, go official.

We don't offer the official API today. If your use needs it, we'll tell you before you pay. A customer who chose wrong leaves angry, and their number goes with them.

Which way does your business actually use WhatsApp — do customers write first, or do you?

elements.content: Interesting new judgment from the Swiss Federal Supreme Court rejecting a domestic award for wrongfully assuming jurisdiction based on small print on a PDF invoice and GTCs sent by WA.  Thank you Irene Röthlisberger and Mike Kramer

postedAt.postedAgoText: 3 days ago • Visible to anyone on or off LinkedIn

repost.content:
In our latest Legal Update, Michael Kramer and Irene Röthlisberger discuss whether a buyer who received invoices via WhatsApp and indicated that he would pay them thereby also accepted the arbitration clauses appearing for the first time in the attached documents. In decision 4A_237/2026 of 14 September 2026, the Swiss Federal Supreme Court distinguished between satisfying the statutory text-form requirement and establishing the parties’ consent to arbitration, taking into account the informal nature of communication via WhatsApp.
 
Key Takeaways:
- An arbitration agreement may, in principle, be concluded through WhatsApp. No signature is required.
- An invoice ordinarily requests payment; it does not create or amend contract terms. An arbitration clause appearing for the first time in an invoice or its attachments does not automatically become part of a contract already concluded.
- Whether a subsequent statement or message amounts to acceptance of an arbitration clause depends on its context, including the communication channel used. An indication that an invoice will be paid does not necessarily establish consent to an arbitration clause contained in the invoice or its attachments.
 
Read more in our Legal Update: https://lnkd.in/eqRxYYkZ

A customer DMs you on Instagram, asks about delivery on WhatsApp, gets their receipt by email, then wants to talk to a person. To them it's one conversation. For most teams, it's four tools and four half-finished records.

That's the gap we've been closing. UnifiedSend now runs WhatsApp, WhatsApp Calls and Voice Calls, email through Resend, SMS, Telegram, Instagram and Facebook Messenger from one platform.

Having more channels isn't really the point. What matters is how you use them together:

Each channel still has its own rules. Instagram and Messenger only let you reply inside a window after the customer messages you. Telegram bots can't start a chat. Marketing email and texts need consent. One platform doesn't remove those rules, but it makes them much easier to follow.

elements.content:
I reviewed 285 business website records in the Miami-Dade area.

190 listed a phone number.
63 listed WhatsApp.

That's 67% vs. 22%.

Here's what caught my attention.

More than 70% of Miami-Dade residents are Hispanic. And according to Pew Research Center, 56% of Hispanic adults in the U.S. use WhatsApp.

That doesn't mean local customers necessarily want to contact businesses through WhatsApp. But it does make me wonder whether businesses are offering the communication channels their customers actually prefer.

And there's another side to this.

Adding a contact channel is easy. Making sure someone responds consistently, especially outside business hours, is an operational challenge.

The goal isn't to offer every possible channel. It's to offer the ones customers value and make them work reliably.

For business owners: are your customers asking for WhatsApp, or are phone calls and text messages still doing the job?


About the data: The review covered 283 unique business websites across 14 categories, with two sites appearing in more than one category (285 records). All were in the Miami-Dade area. I counted phone numbers and WhatsApp links or numbers displayed on home and contact pages. JavaScript-loaded buttons may have been missed. This measures what websites display, not customer preferences or actual response times.

Sources: Pew Research Center, Social Media Use in 2025; U.S. Census Bureau, QuickFacts: Miami-Dade County, Florida.

elements.content:
WhatsApp has an official API, just not for your own account.

The Business Platform is for businesses messaging customers through Meta.
If you want to read and send messages on your personal number from code, you're on your own.

The open source world already solved the hard part.
whatsmeow speaks the multi-device protocol, and wuzapi wraps it as a gateway.

whatsapp-link is the Rust side of that.
It runs wuzapi as a child process, talks to it over stdio with JSON-RPC, and gives you typed chats, messages, reactions and events.

Link it like any other device: scan a QR code in the terminal, or type an 8-character pair code if there's no camera handy.
Then status, chats, history, send, and a watch command that streams incoming messages as JSON lines.

A fair warning, because it matters here.
Unofficial clients can get a WhatsApp account restricted or banned.
Use a number you can afford to lose, keep the volume low, and never use it for bulk messaging.

It's GPL-3.0 and not affiliated with WhatsApp or Meta.

What would you automate first if your own messages had an API?

We built a WhatsApp Business agent workspace on Laravel + Filament.
Three lessons you won’t find in the docs:
1. Let the 24-hour window drive the UI. Inside it you can reply with free text; after it, only approved templates. If the window closes mid-reply, the draft survives. AI reads the conversation and picks the template, filling the variables from context. A human always presses send.
2. Telegram beats a separate app for your team. One group, a topic per customer with Take / Transfer / Close buttons. Agents reply from their phone, where they already are.
3. Opt-in is required for any first message, even a service one. Our costliest bug: our own “Annulla” (cancel) button unsubscribed customers forever. Your do-not-contact list must survive both customer data erasure and key rotation.
